newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Jailed Colombian rebel chiefs call for peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Jailed Colombian rebel chiefs call for peace talks.

text.p: Leaders of Colombia's second largest rebel army called on Wednesday for talks with the "most stable sectors of the State and society" in an attempt to end their three-decade-old uprising.

"We consider the time is right to examine and construct different scenarios for peace in Colombia, through talks with the most stable sectors of the State and society," Francisco Galan and Felipe Torres, jailed heads of the Cuban-inspired National Liberation Army (ELN), said in a letter to four Colombian industrialists.

"Never has the political, social and armed conflict been as bitter, intense and deep-rooted as it is now...you cannot remain on the sidelines of this situation because the conflict is deeply affecting your interests," added the document, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters.

The new call for peace talks followed a fresh offensive by the ELN, set up by radical Roman Catholic priests in 1966, and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), Latin America's oldest and largest guerrilla force.

President Ernesto Samper launched a new drive for national reconciliation after the FARC released 70 troops, some of whom it had held prisoner for more than nine months, in a temporarily demilitarized zone of southern Colombia on June 15.
Part of that peace plan included sending envoys to make contact with rebel leaders.
But after a helicopter was shot down last Sunday -- leaving 20 soldiers and a civilian dead -- even Samper cast doubts on the viability of a fresh peace process.
"Some subversives are afraid of peace and of sitting down at the negotiating table to achieve what they think they can achieve by the blind use of weapons," Samper said this week.
In Wednesday's letter, Galan and Torres described the downing of the helicopter as an "act of war" not "terrorism" as the military and the government described it.
